newsitem.title: UK: Patten affair casts smokescreen over UK politics.
newsitem.headline: Patten affair casts smokescreen over UK politics.

text.p: Oriental intrigue came a poor second to British political streetfighting on Tuesday after party media managers got their hands on the affair of the alleged Hong Kong secrets.

Former Hong Kong governor Chris Patten's denial that he had leaked details of a secret British deal with China to postpone democratic reforms was overshadowed by accusations that the Labour government was fixing the news.

The unseemly spat highlighted apparent divisions, swiftly denied by Conservative former foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind, between the Foreign Office and Patten ahead of the colony's return to China at the end of June.

The Labour government was quick to confirm reports that authorities were investigating allegations that Patten had leaked secret documents to broadcaster Jonathan Dimbleby for inclusion in a book about Patten's time as Britain's last governor of Hong Kong.
It later emerged, however, that police were not involved in the inquiry and therefore Patten was extremely unlikely to face court action under the Official Secrets Act, as had been suggested.
It was minister without portfolio Peter Mandelson, Labour's chief spin doctor, who announced that the inquiry into the Patten affair would be conducted "in a proper, objective and authoritative way".

And it was Mandelson who was blamed for giving fresh life to the story just as news emerged that Foreign Secretary Robin Cook was leaving his wife of 28 years after a secret love affair with his secretary.

The Patten story also succeeded in diverting attention from an embarrassing by-election defeat for the ruling Labour Party in Uxbridge, west of London, a bare two months after Labour crushed the Conservatives in a general election landslide.
"Mandelson accused of fixing the news," read the front-page headline in The Times. "Tories attack Labour's charade of spin," said The Independent.
Attempts to shed light on whether Dimbleby did indeed receive leaked documents meanwhile seemed doomed to failure.

Dimbleby refused to divulge his sources. Instead, he joined numerous calls for an inquiry into events surrounding Britain's dealings with China over the return of the colony after 156 years of British rule.
"Britain's reputation is at stake," Dimbleby declared in a BBC radio interview on Tuesday. "The only way we will establish what really happened and clear this matter up is to have some such inquiry."

London and Beijing began formal negotiations on the return of Hong Kong in 1982, produced an outline treaty in 1984 and then spent the next 13 years sorting out the details. Some of those details, notably on the extent of democratic reforms, aroused great controversy.

Until 1992 Patten was a leading Conservative Party politician, stage-managing John Major's surprise win over Labour in that year's general election but losing his own seat in the process. The Hong Kong governorship was his reward.

Dimbleby's book, "The Last Governor", revealed Patten's anger when he discovered what was alleged to be a "gents' understanding" reached years before between Britain and China, under which Beijing would be allowed to break a promise to move to direct elections after it retook control of Hong Kong.

His determination to introduce direct elections to Hong Kong's legislature ahead of the handover brought him into direct and acrimonious conflict with China -- and with a number of senior British figures involved in the earlier negotiations.
Beijing formally disbanded the elected assembly in the early hours of July 1.
